item.title: EP4 | Nat Commun | John H. McGee: Trimerizer Peptides: Teaching E3 Ligases New Targets
item.description:
Human cells have about 600 E3 ubiquitin ligases, but targeted protein degradation uses only a handful of them — most E3 surfaces are large and flat, with no pocket for a small molecule. A team from FOG Pharmaceuticals and Harvard reports a general method for discovering stapled alpha-helical peptides, "trimerizer" Helicons, that cooperatively glue an E3 ligase to a new target protein without needing a known binder to either. Two phage screens produced trimerizers for CHIP-TEAD4, CHIP-PPIA, and MDM2-beta-catenin, with crystal structures showing direct E3-target contacts — though all the data are in vitro, and degradation has not yet been shown.
Paper: Tokareva, O. S. et al. "Recognition and reprogramming of E3 ubiquitin ligase surfaces by α-helical peptides." Nature Communications (2023). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-42395-z

item.title: EP3 | Cell Chemical Biology | Christina M. Woo: The Degron, Rebuilt as a Warhead
item.description:
In 2022, Christina Woo's group at Harvard showed that cereblon (CRBN) naturally reads a small chemical tag: a C-terminal cyclic imide that forms when glutamine or asparagine residues age. In this follow-up study, the team asks the obvious next question. If the tag is the natural ligand, can you rebuild it as a drug warhead? The answer is the cyclimids, a class of degron-inspired CRBN binders that turn out to be tunable, predictable, and remarkably clean. Built as short dipeptides ending in a cyclic imide ring, forty BRD4 degraders showed the five-membered ring binds CRBN more tightly than the six-membered one, and a quantitative TR-FRET platform measuring the ternary complex directly predicted degradation in cells.
Paper: Ichikawa, S. et al. "The cyclimids: Degron-inspired cereblon binders for targeted protein degradation." Cell Chemical Biology (2024). DOI: 10.1016/j.chembiol.2024.01.003

item.title: EP2 | Nature | Christina M. Woo: The Degron Thalidomide Was Copying
item.description:
Thalidomide and lenalidomide work by binding cereblon (CRBN), the substrate adapter of the CRL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase, and redirecting it to destroy new proteins. But CRBN is an ancient, conserved protein that predates these drugs by hundreds of millions of years. What does it recognize on its own? A team from Harvard University and the University of Southern California, led by Christina M. Woo, reports that the natural signal is a C-terminal cyclic imide — a chemical tag that forms spontaneously when glutamine or asparagine residues at the end of a protein cyclize. The finding, published in Nature, identifies the endogenous degron that thalidomide mimics, and reframes CRBN as a quality-control system that clears damaged proteins.
Paper: Ichikawa, S. et al. "The E3 ligase adapter cereblon targets the C-terminal cyclic imide degron." Nature (2022). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-022-05333-5

item.title: EP1 | Nature | Christina M. Woo: CRBN's Hidden Pocket: A Volume Knob for Protein Degradation
item.description:
Every drug that works through cereblon (CRBN) binds to the same pocket, the thalidomide-binding domain. A team from Harvard University, Scripps Research, and GSK now reports a second, hidden pocket on CRBN. A small molecule that binds this allosteric site, SB-405483, makes orthosteric drugs bind ten times more tightly and tunes their degradation outcomes up or down depending on the target. The finding, published in Nature, is the first cooperative allosteric ligand described for an E3 ubiquitin ligase.
Paper: Dippon, V. N. et al. "Identification of an allosteric site on the E3 ligase adapter cereblon." Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-025-09994-w
